c2.examples.title: Connecting studies in a literature review
c2.examples.typing: "How do I connect these two studies in my literature review?"
c2.examples.thinking: I need to find a way to connect these two studies for my literature review. One is about municipal mergers and local democratic participation, the other is about the digitalisation of public services and citizens' trust in government. My professor said the transition between paragraphs matters a lot. I tried linking the paragraphs through "institutional trust" but it felt too vague. I want something more specific but I am not sure what that would look like.
c2.examples.processing: Full text of both papers is processed. Themes, findings, methodologies, theoretical frameworks all extracted. The most statistically likely "helpful" response pattern for "connect these two studies" is activated. → Generate a comprehensive answer covering multiple possible connection points: shared concepts, overlapping populations, complementary findings, theoretical alignment. Present them as options. Sound confident and thorough.

c2.examples.title: Creating practice questions
c2.examples.thinking: My exam is next week and I want to test myself on chapter 4. The professor always writes tricky MCQs where two options look almost the same and you have to know the exact definition to tell them apart. I need questions that are at that level, not the easy ones where you can guess by elimination.
c2.examples.processing: Full chapter text is processed. Key concepts, definitions, and relationships identified. "MCQ" triggers a default format: one correct answer, three distractors, medium difficulty, recall focused. → Generate questions that cover the chapter evenly, make distractors plausible but clearly distinguishable from the correct answer.

c2.examples.title: Summarizing a paper
c2.examples.thinking: I read this paper but I am not sure I understood the method section. I think they used a between subjects design but the way they describe the groups is confusing. I do not need a full summary, I just need someone to explain the design so I can figure out whether their conclusion actually follows from it.
c2.examples.processing: Full paper is processed. All sections weighted. "Summarize" triggers a default structure: background, aim, method, key findings, conclusion. Roughly equal coverage across sections. → Produce something that reads like a complete, balanced overview. Sound clear and organized.

c2.examples.title: Understanding a concept
c2.examples.thinking: The professor used the term "street-level bureaucracy" in the lecture today and I kind of got it from context, but when I tried to explain it to my friend I couldn't. I think it has something to do with how civil servants implement policies in practice, but I am not sure how this differs from simply having policy discretion or just being an implementing officer.
c2.examples.processing: A definition request. "Street-level bureaucracy" is a well represented concept in the training data. → Generate a clear, textbook style definition. Add an example. Possibly mention related terms. Present a self contained explanation, covering the concept broadly rather than targeting any specific point of confusion.

c2.examples.title: Asking for feedback on your writing
c2.examples.typing: "What do you think of this? Any feedback?"
c2.examples.thinking: I spent two hours on this introduction and I think the argument flows okay, but the last sentence feels weak. My tutor told me last time that I tend to state things too broadly without committing to a clear position. I want to know if I am doing that again here, specifically in the last two sentences.
c2.examples.processing: A paragraph is provided. Feedback requested with no specific focus. → Scan for grammar, clarity, structure, and argument strength across the entire paragraph. Generate a balanced set of comments covering multiple aspects. Highlight positives first, then suggest improvements. Distribute attention evenly across the whole text.

c2.examples.title: What you are actually thinking
c2.examples.typing: "Help me write a motivation letter for an internship in policy development"
c2.examples.thinking: I am applying for this internship in a municipality's policy department, and I really want it because the supervisor was involved in a reorganisation that I read about for my thesis. I have some relevant experience from my research methods course as a small policy evaluation project I completed with a classmate, but I am not sure if that counts. The deadline is tomorrow and I saw that they value "independent thinkers" but I do not want to sound arrogant.
c2.examples.processing: A motivation letter for an internship in policy development. No specific municipality,department, no field, no applicant background, no deadline pressure, no tone preference. → Generate a polished, general purpose motivation letter template. Use broadly applicable language about "passion for public policy" and "eagerness to learn." Structure it in a standard format. Sound professional and enthusiastic.

c2.sat_example.note: The example ends here, but the S.A.T process does not have to stop here. If the student feels that the idea still needs to be developed or wants to ask for feedback, they can start another Self–Team or Self–AI cycle.

steps.name: Intent
steps.text: A student wants to write their literature review about political participation. They are interested in why young people are less likely to vote than older people and has a rough idea of what the research research question could be: Why do young people vote less? However, they are unsure whether this is specific enough for the assignment.

steps.name: Operationalize
steps.text: The student asks AI how they could make their research question more specific. AI suggests considering different types of political participation, different types of elections, and different explanations for differences in voting behaviour.

steps.name: Judge
steps.text: The student considers these possibilities and decides that they will focus on young people's trust in political institutions. Their new research question is: Why do young people vote less, and does trust in political institutions play a role in this relationship?

steps.name: Refine
steps.text: The student asks AI to help refine the wording of their research question without changing what they want to investigate. AI suggests avoiding a clear assumption in the first question and changing the second question from a yes/no question to an open question, in order to be able to give a broader explanation. The student uses this input to formulate a new, specific research question independently: To what extent does young people's trust in political institutions explain their lower levels of political participation?

steps.name: Present
steps.text: In class, the student shares their research question with their classmates and asks for their feedback.

steps.name: Feedback
steps.text: Overall, the student’s classmates understand the idea and think the topic is interesting. One classmate points out that the question seems to assume that lower trust in political institutions is the main explanation for differences in political participation, whereas there may be other relevant explanations.

steps.name: Integrate
steps.text: The student agrees with their classmate and decides to reformulate the research question. They will explore the general association between young people's trust in political institutions and their political participation, without making any a priori assumption about direct causal relationship.

steps.name: Expand
steps.text: The student and their classmates discuss the research question further. Another classmate points out that the relationship might not be straightforward: for example, it could be interesting to consider young people from different socioeconomic backgrounds. This reminds the student of something discussed in class, and she decides to incorporate ir into her research question: To what extent is trust in political institutions associated with political participation among young people, and what role does socioeconomic background play in this relationship? The student is now happy with their research question and ready to start planning the literature search.
